Ever since their emancipation in 1838, conditions in Jamaica had been worsening for the black freedmen. In $YEAR$ there were several floods which ruined many crops, as well as a decade in which the island had been overwhelmed by plagues of cholera and smallpox. Several bankruptcies were declared in the sugar industry, causing a loss of jobs and widening the economic void. 

Consequently tensions between white farmers and ex-slaves increased, and rumors began circulating among the freedmen that white planters intended to restore slavery.
A Letter from Dr. Edward Underhill

In $YEAR$, Dr. Edward Underhill, Secretary of the Baptist Missionary Society of Great Britain, wrote a letter to the Colonial Office in London in order to describe Jamaica's poor state of affairs for the mass of people. This letter was later shown to Governor John Eyre, who tried to deny the truth of its statements. Jamaica's poor blacks learned of the letter and began organizing in "Underhill Meetings." Peasants sent a petition to Queen Victoria asking for Crown lands to cultivate, saying they could not find land for themselves. It sent to Eyre first, and he enclosed a letter with his own comments.

The Queen's reply was made known, and many of the poor believed that Eyre had influenced her opinion: she encouraged the poor to work harder, rather than offering any help. George William Gordon, a wealthy mixed-race politician began encouraging the people in his parish to find ways to make their grievances known.
